displayQuote: I did then what I knew how to do. Now that I know better, I do better

meta.title: Who really said "I did then what I knew how to do. Now that I know better, I do better"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely shared as Maya Angelou, but no source documents this wording — she said it in the second person, to Oprah Winfrey, and it was reported in 1995.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I did then what I knew how to do. Now that I know better, I do better'?
meta.ogDescription: The thought is Angelou’s; this wording is not. What she is documented as saying is second person, and reached print in January 1995.

answer.label: Not Angelou’s wording — a first-person rewrite
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Angelou’s — but this is not how she said it. Every documented version addresses someone else — none is first person: private counsel she gave Oprah Winfrey, first reported when Winfrey recounted it on air — “You did then what you knew how to do and when you knew better you did better.” Quote Investigator ↗ dates that remark to 1995 and traces only second-person forms; the “I did then… I do better” version appears nowhere in its investigation, and we found no source for it either.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: “I did then what I knew how to do. Now that I know better, I do better.”
“You did then what you knew how to do and when you knew better you did better.”
‘Oprah Reveals On Her Show She Smoked Crack Cocaine During Her 20s,’ Jet, 30 January 1995
Maya Angelou (1928–2014), as quoted by Oprah Winfrey

source.excerpt: [Oprah Winfrey, on air, recalling what Angelou said after she confessed her shame:] “You did then what you knew how to do and when you knew better you did better.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that the shorter saying ‘If you know better you should do better’ was circulating by 1958, with variants earlier, and that Oprah Winfrey credited Maya Angelou with the longer remark in 1995 — the version it prints is “You did what you knew how to do, and when you knew better, you did better.”

Wikiquote lists the line among Angelou’s quotations as “You did in your twenties what you knew how to do, and when you knew better you did better,” sourced only ‘as quoted by Oprah Winfrey,’ and notes it is “often misquoted” as ‘Do the best you can until you know better. Then, when you know better, do better’ — see Maya Angelou on Wikiquote ↗.
The first-person version that circulates online carries no source whatsoever: Goodreads files it under its own ‘attributed-no-source’ and ‘unsourced’ tags, with no book named — the entry ↗.
Winfrey repeated the credit to Angelou in her 2014 collection What I Know for Sure (Quote Investigator cites the chapter ‘Power,’ p. 191); the book is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ second person, past tense — consolation offered to someone else, not a statement about oneself
source.excerptNote: Winfrey said the words came from Angelou after she shared her “great shame” over having smoked crack cocaine in her twenties, and that the response turned her life around. The wording shifts between retellings — the Washington Post report drops ‘then,’ and Wikiquote’s version reads ‘You did in your twenties what you knew how to do’ — which is itself a sign that no fixed primary text exists.
source.rightsNote: No copyright status can be asserted for the popular first-person wording, because no source for it has ever been identified. The line Angelou is documented as saying reached print in January 1995 news reporting (Jet and The Washington Post) and is therefore not in the public domain — quote it briefly, with attribution.

author.name: Maya Angelou
author.heading: About Maya Angelou
author.bio: Maya Angelou (born Marguerite Annie Johnson, 1928–2014) was an American memoirist, poet and civil-rights activist, best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969) and for reciting ‘On the Pulse of Morning’ at Bill Clinton’s 1993 inauguration. She met Oprah Winfrey in the late 1970s, when Winfrey was a television anchor in Baltimore, and became her mentor and close friend — the relationship that produced this quotation, which reached the public as remembered private counsel rather than as published prose. Angelou’s fame has also made her one of the most misquoted writers online, which is exactly why separating her documented words from smoothed rewrites is worth the trouble.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source documents the first-person wording. The line as documented: “Oprah Reveals On Her Show She Smoked Crack Cocaine During Her 20s,” Jet, 30 January 1995, 51–52 (Chicago: Johnson Publishing Company); and Patrice Gaines, “How Oprah’s Confession Tumbled Out,” The Washington Post, 13 January 1995, B1. Investigated in Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: You Did What You Knew How To Do, and When You Knew Better, You Did Better,” 30 November 2022.

misattribution.heading: The wording problem
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual. The thought really does trace to Maya Angelou — but the sentence people share is not a sentence anyone has documented her saying. Along the way it changed person, tense and purpose.

items.who: “I did then what I knew how to do…”
items.why: Angelou’s documented words are second person — advice to Winfrey, not a statement about herself. Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ traces only second-person forms and never addresses the first-person version at all, and the first-person line sits in quote databases with nothing behind it — tagged ‘unsourced’ on Goodreads ↗.

items.who: “Do the best you can until you know better. Then when you know better, do better”
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists this among the forms the line is “often misquoted” as, alongside ‘When you know better, do better’ and ‘When you know better, you do better.’

Winfrey is the reason the line is famous and is sometimes named as its author — but she credited Angelou both times she used it, on air in 1995 and in her 2014 book What I Know for Sure, as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

items.who: Phil McGraw, Gary Zukav, Ernest Rogers
items.why: McGraw’s 1999 Life Strategies quotes the line and credits Angelou directly, and columnist Ernest Rogers used the shorter ‘if you know better you should do better’ in 1958 — Quote Investigator ↗ examined each of these attributions.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the counsel is Angelou’s, the sentence is not. What is documented — through Winfrey’s 1995 retelling, as traced by Quote Investigator ↗ — is “You did then what you knew how to do and when you knew better you did better.” The first-person version has no source at all.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The line entered the culture through a confession. In 1995 Oprah Winfrey told her television audience about the shame she felt over her “dark secret” — that she had smoked crack cocaine in her twenties — and said what steadied her was Angelou’s response: that she had done then what she knew how to do, and did better once she knew better. Angelou, whom Winfrey called her ‘mother-sister-friend’ and who dedicated her 1993 essay collection Wouldn’t Take Nothing for My Journey Now to her, was speaking privately, as a mentor, about someone else’s shame.

The rewrite changes what the sentence does. Flipped into the first person — ‘I did then… now that I know better, I do better’ — it stops being consolation you offer to someone else and becomes an affirmation you say about yourself. That shift is probably why the rewrite travelled further than the original: anyone can use it. It is also why the words cannot honestly be presented as Angelou’s.
detailsBody: This is filed as disputed rather than attributed because the specific wording appears in no source at all — not in Angelou’s books, not in the January 1995 press reports, not in Winfrey’s own later retellings. That is a stronger objection than ‘paraphrase’: the grammatical person, the tense and the rhetorical function have all changed.

Even the documented wording is unstable, which tells you there is no fixed primary text: The Washington Post report has “You did what you knew how to do,” Jet has “You did then what you knew how to do,” and Wikiquote carries “You did in your twenties what you knew how to do.” All three are Winfrey remembering a private conversation, not Angelou on the record.
context.pull: She said it about someone else. The internet turned it into something you say about yourself.
